description: AsterNova is a multidisciplinary team driven by curiosity, science, and innovation. We combine diverse skills and perspectives to explore complex challenges through data analysis, computational science, and simulations. Passionate about discovery, we transform scientific ideas into meaningful insights and innovative solutions, pushing boundaries through collaboration and creativity.
summary:
MARSWALK is a browser-based helmet display that helps a Mars astronaut plan and walk an extravehicular activity (EVA) safely in Jezero Crater, explored by NASA's Perseverance rover. It layers NASA orbital terrain (a 20 m CTX elevation model), Perseverance MEDA weather data, and radiation and space-weather context into one 3D map with a slope-aware route, the nearest shelters and live hazard alerts.
Three features target crew safety:
• ASTRA, a voice copilot, answers questions such as "Can I keep walking?" with a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict, the reason and its data source.
• SCOUT-1, a semi-autonomous scout drone inspired by NASA's Ingenuity helicopter, flies ahead, streams video to the visor and samples wind and pressure.
• A charged-dust warning system predicts when a passing dust devil could bring electrically charged dust near the suit, and tells the crew to move aside or take shelter before it arrives.
The first humans on Mars will walk long distances in bulky suits, far from help. MARSWALK turns raw mission data into the route, the risk and the next action, reducing their workload and their exposure.
details:
What does it do?

MARSWALK is a mission planner and helmet heads-up display (HUD) for a crewed EVA in Jezero Crater. It has two screens:

  • Mission console (index.html): the crew picks the science goal, sees the CTX terrain map, the start and goal markers, the planned route and the shelters, and checks a GO / NO-GO briefing before leaving.
  • Helmet visor (eva.html): a first-person 3D view of the terrain with a minimal HUD (oxygen, suit status, heading, distance to goal and to the nearest shelter), the SCOUT-1 drone panel, ASTRA's voice console and the alert banner. A helmet camera saves geotagged photos for the science log.

How does it work?

  1. Terrain. The 20 m CTX digital terrain model of Jezero becomes a 3D mesh. Slope is computed on every cell and used to cost the route, so the path avoids steep ground. A rough-relief layer adds rocks and outcrops at walking scale for training.
  2. Shelters. The browser searches the terrain for sheltered spots (crater walls, low ground) and keeps the nearest one ready as a fallback.
  3. Weather. fetch_meda.py downloads Perseverance MEDA pressure and wind records from NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS) and builds an hourly climatology by local solar time. If the download is unavailable, a bundled fallback climatology is used. On top of it the simulator adds realistic gusts and spawns dust devils at the rate and strength MEDA observed.
  4. SCOUT-1 drone. A six-rotor scout, modeled on Ingenuity-class flight limits, flies ahead, escorts, tracks or surveys. It launches on its own, returns to dock on low battery and keeps clear of dust devils. Its camera is rendered off-screen and shown in the visor; its pressure and wind readings feed ASTRA.
  5. Charged-dust alerts. For every dust devil, the system estimates the electric field from its pressure drop, scales it by distance, and predicts the closest approach to the astronaut. It raises ADVISORY, WARNING or CRITICAL before the dust arrives (model below).
  6. ASTRA copilot. A local reasoning engine recognizes intents (status, oxygen, dust, vortex, weather, drone, shelter, route, terrain, science, sources) and answers by voice with a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict and the reason. Every answer can cite its source ID from the project's source register. An optional large language model adds free-form conversation when an API key is configured; the safety logic does not depend on it.

All four modules report to ASTRA, so the crew gets one verdict instead of four separate readouts. Use this figure on slide 4 and in the README.

The charged-dust model used for the alerts, with Δp the dust-devil core pressure drop in Pa, r the distance to the astronaut and R the vortex radius:

Thresholds: ADVISORY at 2 kV/m or more, WARNING at 8, CRITICAL at 15. Electrical breakdown in Mars air is about 20–25 kV/m, so the alerts fire well below discharge conditions. The coefficients are a modeling choice based on published field measurements of terrestrial dust devils and Mars discharge studies (Farrell et al. 2005; Delory et al. 2006; Harrison et al. 2016); they are not measured on Mars.

A dust devil only raises an alert when it is predicted to arrive within 5 minutes; a WARNING is also forced if its path passes within its own diameter. Use this figure on slide 6.

What benefits does it have?

  • Fewer decisions under stress. The route, the nearest shelter and the verdict are on one screen.
  • Early warning. Alerts are triggered by the predicted closest approach, not by the dust devil's current position, so the crew has time to move.
  • Eyes ahead. The drone sees terrain and weather the astronaut cannot see yet.
  • Traceable answers. Every number ASTRA uses links to a source in the register, and excluded sources are listed with the reason.
  • Runs anywhere. It is a web app with a small Python server; no install beyond Python and a browser.

What do we hope to achieve?

A prototype of the cockpit-style tool the first Mars crews will need: one that turns NASA data into a route, a risk and an action. Next steps are to run the full MEDA record across more sols and seasons, add more landing sites with CTX or HiRISE terrain, and test the HUD with users in suit-like conditions (gloves, limited field of view).

Tools, languages and software

Layer

Tools

3D rendering and UI

JavaScript, Three.js r161, HTML5, CSS

Voice

Web Speech API (en-US speech recognition and synthesis)

Server

Python 3 http.server on port 8010 (/api/status, /api/assistant, /api/photo)

Data processing

Python (fetch_media.py), JSON data files

Storage

Indexed DB in the browser plus a local fotos_eva/ folder

Optional AI

OpenAI API for free-form conversation (key kept in a local .env, never published)
